title: Resilience ladder routing playbook
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a practical, implementable pattern we are calling the 'resilience ladder' for inference routing: a prioritized sequence of fallback options that the control plane will evaluate when a request cannot be served by the primary path. It covers policy primitives, model variant families, tiered capacity semantics, multi-region spillover mechanics, and the monitoring/telemetry required to operate safely.

Scope
- Focus: production inference traffic (hosted + dedicated).
- Includes: routing policy design, control-plane decision points, config examples, tests and runbook hooks.
- Excludes: billing and pricing changes, deep runtime kernel work (covered in serving-runtime).

Motivation & goals
- Keep p99 latency SLOs as stable as possible while degrading output quality gracefully.
- Provide predictable cost bounds during degraded conditions.
- Ensure customer isolation (dedicated pools) and compliance when required.
- Make routing decisions auditable and reversible.

Key constraints
- Heterogeneous model variants (FP16, int8, quantized, distilled) have different quality/cost/latency profiles.
- Cross-region spillover must respect data residency and VPC constraints.
- Control-plane decisions must be computable in <5ms for per-request routing paths.
- Rollouts and fallbacks must be safe: automated fallbacks allowed only under monitored SLO breaches.

Terminology
- primary: the route/model chosen by the service-level config (customer pin).
- variant family: a group of compatible model artifacts varying in perf/quality (e.g., llama-70b-fp16, llama-70b-quant4).
- ladder rung: an ordered fallback option (same-region cheaper variant -> dedicated spare pool -> regional spillover -> degraded-mode model).
- reserved capacity: capacity committed to a tenant or route (no preemption).
- opportunistic capacity: best-effort lower-cost capacity that can be revoked.

Resilience ladder (high-level)
1) Local primary (reserved, pinned model variant)
2) Local cheap variant (same family, quantized, same latency SLO)
3) Local batched/opportunistic fallback (increases latency but reduces cost)
4) Dedicated overflow pool in-region (shared failover reserved capacity)
5) Cross-region spillover to nearest compliant region (respecting data residency)
6) Degraded-mode small-model (CPU or tiny GPU) with strict token limits and explicit quality flag in response
7) Reject with graceful error and suggested retry/backoff

Policy primitives for the control plane
- score(route) -> float: computed at request time from vector of features: model_cost_per_token, current_qps_util, avg_latency, estimated_kv_cache_hit, region_penalty, customer_priority.
- hard_constraints: {data_residency_ok, vpc_ok, model_signature_compatible} -> boolean
- budget_guardrail: per-tenant cost per-minute threshold to avoid runaway spending when fallback paths are expensive.
- tempo_window: short-term state (60s) used to prevent flapping between rungs.

Example score function (pseudocode)
score = w1*latency_headroom_pct + w2*(1 - cost_normalized) + w3*cache_affinity - w4*region_latency_penalty + w5*priority_bonus
Routes are then ranked; the control plane picks the highest scoring route that satisfies hard_constraints and budget_guardrail.

Model variant families and compatibility matrix
- Family id: llama-70b-v1
  - variants: fp16 (high-quality), int8-quant (cost-optimized), 4bit-distil (fast-small), cpu-tiny (degraded)
- Compatibility: we require tokenization, output schema, and tool-calling contract compatibility for automatic fallbacks. If not compatible, skip to next rung.

Tiered capacity semantics
- RESERVED: never preempted for the tenant; used by primary routes.
- BURST: short-lived scale-ups tied to autoscaling groups; may be reclaimed after a cooldown.
- OPPORTUNISTIC: low-cost capacity on cheaper instances; can be preempted at any time.
- SHARED_FAILOVER_POOL: cross-tenant reserved pool with routing arbitration based on priority and market (used only for emergencies).

Cross-region spillover rules
- Eligibility: route marked spillover_allowed AND data_residency_ok for target region.
- Preference: prefer nearest region by latency and cost; apply region_penalty factor to score.
- Bandwidth throttle: global spillover qps cap per origin region to avoid cascades. Default 5% of origin region capacity.
- Circuit-breaker: if target region exceeds 70% of its capacity due to spillover, stop accepting new spillover requests for that origin for 5 minutes.

Cache & prefix affinity considerations
- KV cache reuse is a primary reason to prefer same-region / same-variant routing. Policy should include cache_affinity score term that penalizes variant mismatch when estimated_cache_hit_loss > 0.1.
- For spillover, consider synthetic warm-up: async pre-warm KV entries for top n prompts per customer when spillover first occurs.

Degraded-mode responses and UX
- When returning results from degraded small models, include a \"degraded\": true flag and a short quality_hint (\"reduced detail\", \"higher hallucination risk\").
- Offer client-side suggestions: reduce max_tokens, split long sessions, or schedule non-urgent work for off-peak.

Operational signals and telemetry
- Per-route metrics: qps, 95/99/999 latency, per-token cost, model-variant usage breakdown, cache_hit_rate, fallback_rate (percent of requests not served by primary).
- Control-plane decisions log: request_id -> chosen_rung, score_breakdown, constraints_failed. Store 30 days in hot path for debugging; 365 days in cold storage.
- Alerts: fallback_rate > 1% sustained for 3m -> page on-call; spillover qps > 10% of origin -> page SRE.

Runbook snippets (for on-call)
- Symptom: sudden spike in fallback_rate for region us-west1
  1) Check control-plane decision logs for common failed constraints (concurrency limit vs reserved exhaustion).
 2) If reserved capacity exhausted, trigger autoscale for SHARED_FAILOVER_POOL (runbook link: CONFLUENCE-PL/Failover-Pools).
 3) If cross-region spillover triggered, verify data_residency flags; temporarily set spillover.allowed=false for impacted products until mitigation.

Config example (YAML style - policy fragment)
- name: customer-route:acme-platform
  primary_variant: llama-70b-v1/fp16
  ladder_rungs:
    - type: same_variant_cheaper
      max_latency_ms: 250
      allowed_variants: [int8-quant, 4bit-distil]
    - type: opportunistic_batch
      max_latency_ms: 600
      batch_window_ms: 40
    - type: shared_failover_pool
      priority_threshold: 80
    - type: cross_region_spillover
      allowed_regions: [us-east1, us-west1, europe-west1]
      max_spillover_percent: 5
    - type: degraded_cpu_model
      max_tokens: 128

Testing plan (automated)
- Unit tests: score function with synthetic traffic patterns.
- Integration: chaos-tests that drain reserved pools and assert fallback ladder decisions and telemetry correctness.
- Load test: incremental ramp to force cross-region spillover and assert circuit-breaker behavior.

Operational tradeoffs & notes
- Quality vs latency: adding cheaper local variants will keep latency but reduce quality; must provide customers explicit opt-in for any quality reduction when pinned.
- Cost vs availability: shared_failover_pool provides availability guarantees but increases reserved spending; thresholding and priority arbitration is required.
- Complexity: more rungs increases decision surface; we must keep the control-plane deterministic and debuggable.

Open questions (owner in parentheses)
- How to express per-prompt importance (e.g., high-priority system prompts) in score without expensive per-token compute? (Diego)
- Should we expose fallback hints to customers in realtime (and allow them to opt-out)? Legal/privacy implications? (Aisha)
- Safe defaults for max_spillover_percent per region given current federated capacity map? (Platform capacity team)

Next steps and action items
- Implement score telemetry exporter (ENG-7142) (Maya, now)
- Prototype opportunistic batch runner and integrate with ladder (PR referenced above) (Liam)
- Run a chaos test that simulates reserved pool drain for a single high-traffic tenant and validate ladder behavior (Diego)

Appendix: quick example decision trace (simulated)
- input: request R123 from us-west1, tenant T=acme, primary reserved pool at 100%, local cheapest variant at 80% but incompatible with tool-calls -> control-plane evaluates rungs:
  - rung1 (primary) -> fails (reserved saturated)
  - rung2 (same family quant) -> fails (contract_incompatible = true)
  - rung3 (opportunistic batch) -> passes constraints, score=0.62 -> selected.
  - telemetry emits fallback_rate++, chosen_rung=opportunistic_batch, score_breakdown=[latency_headroom:0.2,cost:0.7,affinity:0.1]

If you want, I can convert this into a Confluence-ready page, extract a minimal YAML policy template for the control-plane API, or draft a test plan for the chaos-run.
